title: The Road Racing Guide
subtitle: A field guide to choosing, preparing for, and riding your road event.
meta_description: Eight free chapters on road event selection, training, workout execution, fueling, group riding, race week, and recovery.

chapters.title: What Is Road Racing?
chapters.subtitle: Fondos, sportives, and the events you're actually training for

blocks.content: A gran fondo, sportive, or century gives you a route and a day to prepare for. Your goal might be finishing, improving your time, or staying with a particular group. Name that goal before you start comparing plans.
The group changes the ride. Practise predictable riding, communication, and looking ahead before you rely on drafting in an event. Follow the organiser’s rules and leave room to react. [^group]
Use these chapters as a reference. Your training history, available time, and course demands determine the workouts you need.

blocks.title: Name the goal
rows: Repeatable riding, pacing, food and refill practice
Identify where you lost time before adding intensity
Group riding practice and the ability to pace climbs

items.label: Gran fondo or sportive
items.detail: A long route, feed stations, and groups moving at different speeds. Your pacing and group choices need to last for the whole day.

items.label: Century
items.detail: Completing the distance is the goal. Prepare your contact points, food, refill plan, and time on the bike.

items.label: Criterium or circuit race
items.detail: Repeated corners, accelerations, and positioning. Practise the skills in a controlled setting before entering a fast bunch.

items.label: Time trial
items.detail: You ride against the clock. Rehearse pacing, the course, and a position you can sustain.

sources.title: British Cycling — Guide to riding in a group

chapters.title: Choosing Your Race
chapters.subtitle: Pick the event that fits your engine and your calendar

blocks.content: Read the route before you pick the race. Distance tells part of the story. Long climbs, technical descents, exposed roads, and feed-zone spacing change how you prepare.

Put your goal events on the same calendar as work and travel. Two A races need recovery and rebuilding between them. A second race is a planning decision, more than another taper pasted onto the first.
Check the organiser’s current route, start arrangements, cutoffs, and mandatory equipment. If a detail is unconfirmed, keep it marked unconfirmed.

blocks.title: Read the course
rows: How long do you expect to be riding?
Can you ride them safely within your ability?
What must you carry between refills?

sections.title: Choose the course, then the race

items.label: Sustained climbs
items.detail: Read the climb lengths and gradients. Choose gearing before you discover its limits on race day.

items.label: Repeated short climbs
items.detail: Expect repeated changes in effort; practise pacing the transition back onto the flat.

items.label: Technical descents
items.detail: Course familiarity and controlled cornering matter. A climbing result does not establish descending skill.

items.label: Exposed roads
items.detail: Wind can change group selection. Keep your route and road position within the organiser’s rules.

chapters.title: Building the Engine
chapters.subtitle: Base, then build — the aerobic foundation under everything

blocks.content: Build a week you can repeat. Easy riding should leave room for the harder workouts and the rest of your life. A long ride matters, but it does not excuse missing every other workout.

Use the plan’s purpose to choose your effort. Research on trained endurance athletes describes substantial low-intensity training alongside smaller amounts of harder work; it does not give every rider the same percentage split. [^intensity]
When fatigue accumulates, look at the whole week before adding more. Review sleep, workout completion, and how your legs respond. Progression needs to fit the work you can absorb.

blocks.title: Read the week
rows: Could you keep the effort controlled?
Did you complete the prescribed work?
Did your pacing and fueling hold up?
Did fatigue improve before the next workout?

sections.title: The Foundational Model: How Adaptation Works

blocks.content: All training follows the same basic cycle. Understanding this cycle is the difference between training intelligently and just accumulating fatigue.

steps.label: Stress
steps.content: You apply training stress—a hard workout that exceeds your current capacity. This creates disruption: muscle fibers develop microtears, glycogen stores deplete, metabolic waste accumulates, cellular damage occurs. Your body registers this as a problem that needs solving.

steps.label: Fatigue
steps.content: Immediately after training, you're weaker than before you started. Your muscles are damaged. Your fuel tanks are empty. Your nervous system is taxed. If you tested your {{FTP}} right after a hard interval workout, it would be lower than your rested FTP. This is normal. Fatigue is the signal that triggers adaptation.

steps.label: Recovery
steps.content: Given adequate rest, nutrition, and time, your body initiates repair: muscle fibers rebuild, mitochondria multiply, capillary density increases, glycogen storage expands, neurological efficiency improves. Timeline: 24-48 hours for muscle repair, 3-7 days for mitochondrial adaptation, 2-4 weeks for new baseline fitness.

steps.label: Supercompensation
steps.content: If recovery is complete, your body doesn't just return to baseline—it overshoots. Your body builds slightly more capacity than it had before to handle similar stress more easily next time. You're now stronger than you were before the workout.

steps.label: Apply New Stress
steps.content: Once you've adapted, you apply a slightly larger stress. The cycle repeats. Over weeks and months, these small adaptations compound into meaningful fitness gains.

blocks.question: What happens if you apply new training stress before recovery is complete?

options.text: You get faster because you're training harder
You accumulate fatigue without adaptation — digging a hole, not building fitness
Your body skips to supercompensation faster

blocks.explanation: Insufficient recovery is the most common training mistake. Without complete recovery, you never reach the supercompensation phase. You're just piling fatigue on top of fatigue.

blocks.content:
**The Practical Rules:**

1. **Training stress must be adequate but not excessive** — Hard enough to trigger adaptation. Not so hard you can't recover.
2. **Recovery must be prioritized as much as training** — Sleep, nutrition, stress management—these aren't optional. They're where adaptation happens.
3. **Consistency compounds** — Ten weeks of steady training beats four weeks of heroics followed by injury or burnout.
4. **Fitness is cumulative** — Every completed workout adds to the total. Missed workouts don't just subtract—they prevent compounding.
5. **Patience is required** — Meaningful adaptation takes weeks and months, not days. Trust the process.

blocks.alt: Supercompensation curve showing stress, fatigue, recovery, and adaptation overshoot
blocks.caption: The foundational model — train, recover, adapt, repeat.

blocks.content: This is the mechanism behind every training gain you will ever make. You stress the system, you let it recover, and it rebuilds slightly stronger than before. Skip the stress and nothing changes. Skip the recovery and you just accumulate damage. The athletes who get this wrong usually err on the recovery side — they train hard enough but never rest enough to let adaptation happen. Respect the curve.
What does 12 weeks of consistent training actually look like? Drag the divider to compare untrained versus trained physiology.

blocks.alt: Establish a baseline, train, and retest
blocks.caption: Read the reference and its qualifications below.

blocks.content: These gains are real and replicable. But they require patience and consistency. Skip weeks, train sporadically, and the before and after look identical.

sections.title: Training Zones: What They Mean and How to Use Them

blocks.content:
Every workout prescription includes a zone target. Here's what they mean and how to use them.

Zones exist to quantify intensity and give you a common language for prescribing workouts.

But here's the paradox: the end goal of measuring intensity is to help you develop a *feeling* for intensity. You use power meters, heart rate monitors, and zone charts to develop an intuitive sense of effort. Because despite our best efforts, the human body remains too complex to neatly summarize with device-generated data. Your subjective feeling is infinitely more valuable than numbered outputs based on incomplete data collection, reductive models, and population-level assumptions.

You're a special snowflake. Learn your snowflake.

blocks.caption: Master Zone Chart
rows: Very easy, relaxed pace. Gentle spinning—feels like nothing. Full conversation possible.
All-day pace—sustainable and steady. Can chat freely. This is where you should spend MOST of your training time.
Comfortably hard. Breathing deeper but rhythmic. Talking in short sentences. Sustainable for 1-2 hours.
Uncomfortably sustainable. Hard enough to hurt, easy enough to repeat. Where you'll spend most of a road event.
Hard, controlled effort. Only a few words at a time. 10-30 minute blocks.
Very hard, heavy breathing. Near maximum. 2-8 minute efforts.
Sharp, explosive efforts—30 seconds to 3 minutes max. All-out.
All-out sprints. Pure explosive power. Lasts only seconds.

blocks.alt: Training zone spectrum showing 7 zones from Z1 Active Recovery to Z7 Neuromuscular with power and heart rate ranges
blocks.caption: The zone spectrum — from recovery spin to redline effort.

blocks.content: Here is the uncomfortable truth: most of your training should be in Zone 2. Boring, conversational, feels-like-nothing Zone 2. The riders who train too hard too often never build the aerobic base that carries them through the final third of a race. Train easy enough that it feels embarrassing. That is the right intensity.
Your power-duration curve defines what you can sustain at different time intervals—from a 5-second sprint to a 6-hour road event. The zones are derived from this curve.

blocks.alt: Power-duration curve showing sustainable watts from 5 seconds to 6 hours with training zone bands overlaid
blocks.caption: The power-duration curve — your physiological fingerprint as a rider.

blocks.content: Training at the right intensity means respecting these boundaries. The curve bends sharply—even a small increase above threshold drops sustainable duration dramatically.

tabs.label: Why G Spot?
tabs.title: Why G Spot, Not Sweet Spot?
tabs.content:
We call it G Spot instead, and it's not just branding:

**1. It's more intensity-specific to road racing** — Sweet Spot (88-93% {{FTP}}) is too high for most road events. Actual race data shows most road eventrs spend the majority of their time at 87-90% FTP. G Spot (88-92%) better matches reality.

**2. It's better for training execution** — Sweet Spot intervals at 90-93% FTP have a nasty habit of turning into threshold intervals. G Spot's lower ceiling (92% max) keeps you honest.

**3. It's equally as scientific** — Frank Overton pointed at a unitless graph showing two theoretical curves and called it science. Two can play that game. G Spot is calibrated to actual road event power data.

**4. It's better named, objectively** — "Sweet Spot" sounds like something your grandmother would say about a parking space.

tabs.label: Three Systems
tabs.title: Three Measurement Systems
tabs.content:
You'll see three metrics in your workouts:

**Power (% of FTP)** — The most precise. Measures actual work output in watts.

**Heart Rate (% of HRmax)** — Secondary system. Lags power by 1-3 minutes, affected by heat, hydration, fatigue, stress, caffeine. Useful for pacing long efforts.

**{{RPE}} (Rate of Perceived Exertion, 1-10 scale)** — Your subjective experience. The ultimate arbiter. If the numbers say one thing but your body says another, trust your body.

**How to set your zones:**

- **FTP:** 20-minute all-out test, multiply average power by 0.95
- **HRmax:** 211 - (0.64 × age). Example: age 38 = 186 bpm
- **RPE:** Practice correlating numbers with feeling

tabs.label: Critical Notes
tabs.title: Critical Notes on Zone Use
tabs.content:
**1. Zones are descriptive, not prescriptive** — They describe what you did, not rigid targets.

**2. Easy means easy** — Most people train too hard on easy days. Zone 2 should feel conversational.

**3. RPE is the ultimate arbiter** — Power meters can lie. Heart rate can be misleading. Your body doesn't lie.

**4. FTP changes slowly** — Don't retest every week. Test at Week 1, optionally Week 6-7, and before your race.

**5. Heart rate lags power** — Use power for short, hard efforts. Use heart rate for pacing long endurance rides.

**6. Anaerobically gifted athletes are different** — The percentages assume average physiology. If you're exceptional, your coach will adjust zones.

blocks.content:
When you manipulate training, you're adjusting three variables: **frequency** (how often), **duration** (how long), and **intensity** (how hard). These create *training load*—the total stress applied to your system.

Thanks to really smart people we can quantify training stress precisely:

blocks.caption: Key Training Load Metrics
rows: Training Stress Score — quantifies total stress of a workout
Lets you compare workouts. 90-min tempo and 60-min VO2max can both = ~80 TSS
Chronic Training Load (42-day average TSS) — your fitness
Higher CTL = more fitness. Builds slowly (up to +5-8 pts/week inside a loading block, netting about +10/month once recovery weeks are counted)
Acute Training Load (7-day average TSS) — your fatigue
High ATL = fresh fatigue. Responds quickly to training changes
Negative = building fitness. Race day target: +15 to +25

blocks.alt: 12-week Performance Management Chart showing CTL fitness, ATL fatigue, and TSB form
blocks.caption: CTL builds slowly. ATL spikes fast. TSB tells you when to race.

blocks.content: The PMC is not a toy — it is the most powerful planning tool in endurance sport. When CTL is climbing steadily and TSB turns positive 10-14 days before race day, you are ready. When CTL flatlines or TSB is deep negative on race week, something went wrong. Check your chart weekly.

sources.title: Seiler and Kjerland (2006) — Quantifying training intensity distribution

chapters.title: Workout Execution
chapters.subtitle: Zones, intervals, and hitting the targets that matter

blocks.content: Read the workout before you ride. Know the target, the recovery between efforts, and the point at which you should stop repeating work you can no longer execute.

Power, heart rate, and perceived effort answer different questions. Use the measurement the workout prescribes and record what happened. If the target becomes unmanageable, write that in the workout comments.
An easy ride and a hard workout should have different purposes. Avoid turning the warm-up, recoveries, and ride home into extra intervals.

blocks.title: Execute the workout
rows: Read targets and recoveries; prepare your route
Prepare for the work without adding hard efforts
Follow the prescribed target and recovery
Record completion, effort, and any problems

items.label: Warm Up Properly
items.detail: For endurance: 10-15 min Z1→Z2. For intensity: 15-20 min Z1→Z2→Z3 with 3×1 min openers. Cold muscles don't produce power efficiently.

items.label: Do the Actual Workout (Not More, Not Less)
items.detail: Execute what's prescribed. Not more. Not less. Trust the plan. Adding volume or intensity might feel productive, but it accumulates fatigue, compromises recovery, and ruins tomorrow's workout.

items.label: Chase Time-in-Zone, Not Hero Intervals
items.detail: Goal: highest average power across the entire set. Start conservatively. Finish strong. Complete the set. Bad: 320W/290W/270W/Failed. Good: 300W/300W/295W/295W.

items.label: Stop If Power Drops >10%
items.detail: Quality beats quantity. Four quality intervals at 300W beats six degraded intervals averaging 270W.

tabs.label: Z2 Endurance
tabs.title: Z2 (Endurance) — The Foundation
tabs.content:
**Target:** 56-75% {{FTP}}, {{RPE}} 3-4, conversational

Ride steady, no surges. Should feel easy enough to go for hours. Full sentences possible. Nose breathing (if you can't, you're too hard).

**Common mistakes:** Drifting into Z3 because you're bored. Turning every endurance ride into a tempo ride. Riding with faster friends and getting pulled up.

**The fix:** Discipline. Easy means easy. This is 70-80% of your training volume. Protect it.

tabs.label: G Spot
tabs.title: G Spot (88-92% FTP) — Gravel Race Pace
tabs.content:
**Target:** 88-92% {{FTP}}, {{RPE}} 6-7, "uncomfortably sustainable"

Stay seated, control breathing. Hard enough to hurt, easy enough to repeat. Could talk in short phrases but wouldn't want to. Fuel properly: 60-80g carbs/hour.

**Common mistakes:** Pushing into threshold (93%+). Not fueling adequately.

**Success looks like:** All intervals completed, power stable ±5%, RPE 6-7, feeling like you could do one more if forced.

tabs.label: Threshold
tabs.title: Threshold (93-105% FTP) — FTP Development
tabs.content:
**Target:** 95-100% {{FTP}}, {{RPE}} 7-8

Goal: 30-60 min total time-in-zone. Even intervals (2×20, 3×15, 4×12) beat one heroic 40-minute effort. Start at 95%, build into rhythm. Recovery: 5-10 min Z1 between intervals.

**Success looks like:** All intervals completed at target, power consistent (±3%), RPE 7-8, interval 3 felt hardest but you finished strong.

tabs.label: VO2max
tabs.title: VO2max (110-120% FTP) — Raising the Ceiling
tabs.content:
**Target:** 110-120% FTP, {{RPE}} 9, gasping, burning legs, maximal but repeatable

Warm-up is critical: 20-25 min progressive with 3×1 min openers. Hit the target from the start. Full recovery between: 4-5 min Z1, HR must drop below 60% max. Stop if power drops >10%.

**Success looks like:** 4-5 quality intervals at target power, RPE 9 throughout, completed the set without falling apart.

items.title: Scenario 1: You Feel Like Shit
items.content:
**Symptoms:** Sleep was bad, work was stressful, legs feel dead before you start

**What to do:** Reduce intensity by 5-10%. Shorten intervals if needed. Prioritize completion over heroics. Swap intensity for endurance if you're really cooked.

**What not to do:** Push through and accumulate junk volume that compromises recovery.

items.title: Scenario 2: You Can't Hit Power Targets
items.content:
**Symptoms:** Interval 1 feels way harder than it should, power is 10W+ below target

**Possible causes:** Stale {{FTP}}, inadequate recovery, illness brewing, equipment issues

**What to do:** Check equipment first. Drop power 5% and see if effort matches RPE. If still struggling, abort and take a rest day. Retest FTP if this happens multiple workouts in a row.

items.title: Scenario 3: Life Happens (Missed Workouts)
items.content:
**What to do:** Don't double up to "make up" missed workouts. Don't panic and add volume. Execute the next workout as scheduled. One missed workout doesn't ruin your plan.

**What not to do:** Try to cram two days into one. That just digs a deeper hole.

blocks.content:
**Green light (execute as written):** Good sleep, resting HR normal, feeling motivated, body feels fresh.

**Yellow light (reduce intensity 5-10%):** Sleep was okay but not great, slight fatigue, moderate motivation.

**Red light (swap intensity for easy ride or rest):** Multiple nights of poor sleep, elevated resting HR, body feels broken, high life stress.

**The rule:** Recovery is not weakness. Training when you're buried just makes you more buried.

blocks.alt: Green/Yellow/Red autoregulation system for daily training decisions
blocks.caption: Check before every workout. Green = go. Yellow = modify. Red = rest.

blocks.content: This framework works because it removes ego from the decision. You are not deciding whether you are tough enough — you are checking objective signals. Resting HR elevated? Sleep wrecked? Those are red signals, not character tests. The athletes who last decades in this sport respect red lights.

blocks.question: During a threshold interval set, your power on interval 3 drops to 88% of target despite maximum effort. What should you do?

options.text: Push harder and finish the set — mental toughness matters
Stop the set — power dropped >10%, quality beats quantity
Add an extra interval at the end to make up for the weak one

blocks.explanation: When power drops more than 10% from target, you're accumulating junk volume, not building fitness. Four quality intervals at target power beats six degraded intervals. Stop, cool down, and recover for the next workout. This is discipline, not quitting.

items.label: Choose the terrain
items.detail: Use a steady climb for sustained work and safe open space for group drills. Choose a repeatable route that fits the workout.

items.label: Keep the work clear
items.detail: Do not count junctions, braking, and coasting as equivalent to completing the prescribed effort.

items.label: Write the useful comment
items.detail: Record what changed the effort. Traffic, gradient, heat, group movement, and fatigue are useful details.

items.label: Review before repeating
items.detail: Change the route or workout execution when the environment prevented the intended work.

chapters.title: Fueling for the Distance
chapters.subtitle: Carbs per hour, hydration, and a gut that can take it

blocks.content: Choose a fueling target for the duration and effort of the ride, then practise it. The Australian Institute of Sport’s guidance allows higher carbohydrate intake for longer endurance events, including up to 90 grams an hour for events beyond roughly 2.5–3 hours. Tolerance and the carbohydrate mix matter. [^fuel]
Use the products you intend to carry. Record what you ate, drank, and tolerated on your long ride. Change the plan during training while you have time to learn from it.
Check where you can refill. Put food and bottles within reach, and decide what you will do if a feed station is crowded or a bottle is lost.

blocks.title: Pack the fuel
rows: Set an intake target you have practised
Know the distance between feed stations
Plan for a missed refill or lost bottle

blocks.content: Your gut is trainable just like your muscles. If you never eat during training rides, your gut won't tolerate eating during races.

steps.label: Weeks 1-4 (Base Phase)
steps.content: Practice eating real food on easy rides. Start with 40-50g carbs per hour, mostly solid. Build tolerance gradually. SGLT1 transporters can double in 2 weeks of consistent gut training (GSSI).

steps.label: Weeks 5-8 (Build Phase)
steps.content: Increase toward your race-day target rate. Mix of liquids and solids. Practice eating at tempo pace. Your gut adapts to what you train it for.

steps.label: Weeks 9-10 (Peak Training)
steps.content: Hit your race-day target rate (see duration-scaled targets in your prep kit). Race nutrition only (gels, drink, bars you'll use on race day). Practice at race pace. For ultra events (12+ hours), include savory and mixed-macro foods alongside gels.

steps.label: Race Week
steps.content: Stick with what worked in training. No new products. Trust your gut (literally).

blocks.content: Most race nutrition failures fall into four predictable categories. Recognizing them before race day is the difference between finishing strong and crawling to the line.

Look at those numbers again: 600 grams of carbohydrates for an 8-hour race. That is 24 gels. When you see it visualized like that, the scale of race fueling stops being abstract. This is why you practice nutrition in training.

items.title: The Optimist
items.content: "Aid stations will have what I need." They won't, or they'll run out. The first 500 riders cleaned out the bananas and Coke at aid station 3. You're rider 1,200. Assume aid stations have nothing you need. Carry enough fuel between stations even if they have everything.

items.title: The Minimalist
items.content: "I'll just eat when I'm hungry." By the time you're hungry, you're already glycogen-depleted. Hunger is a late-stage bonk signal. Fuel by the clock, not by feel. Set a timer for every 20 minutes. Eat something every time it goes off. No negotiation.

items.title: The Experimenter
items.content: "Let me try this new gel flavor on race day." Your gut under race stress is not the time to experiment. That mystery gel from the aid station? Your stomach will rebel at mile 60. Race with exactly what you've trained with. Nothing new on race day. Ever.

items.title: The Denier
items.content: "I don't want to carry that much food." Math check: a 100-mile race takes 6-8 hours. At 75g carbs/hour, that's 450-600g total—roughly 18-24 gels or equivalent. Yes, that much. Most people bring half that and wonder why they bonk at mile 80.

sources.title: Australian Institute of Sport — Sports drinks: how and when

chapters.title: Pack Skills & Race Tactics
chapters.subtitle: Drafting, echelons, positioning, and when to spend

blocks.content: Practise group riding with an experienced group. Ride predictably, communicate hazards, avoid overlapping wheels, and look ahead. The safe gap changes with speed, surface, visibility, and the riders around you. [^group]
Keep every move within the space available to you. Wind and corners change the group’s shape; they do not give you permission to cross the centre line or squeeze through a gap.
Choose your position before an exposed section or climb when you can do so safely. If you lose the group, return to your pacing and fueling plan instead of chasing every surge.

blocks.title: Ride predictably
rows: Avoid overlap and keep space to react
Check space and signal your intention

sections.title: A team-camp approach to group practice

items.label: Agree before riding
items.detail: Choose the route, purpose, roles, signals, and regroup point while everyone can hear.

items.label: Separate the starts
items.detail: For a controlled group exercise, stagger starts so groups are not competing for the same road space.

items.label: Rehearse the leadout
items.detail: Agree who does what and where the effort ends. The exercise is coordinated riding, not surprise manoeuvres.

items.label: Regroup and review
items.detail: Discuss timing and communication after the exercise. Repeat only where the route and supervision allow it.

sources.title: British Cycling — Guide to riding in a group

chapters.title: Race Week
chapters.subtitle: Taper, prep, and arriving sharp instead of stale

blocks.content: A taper reduces accumulated fatigue while retaining some familiar intensity. Research supports reducing training volume before competition, but the length and reduction depend on the athlete and event. Follow your plan rather than copying a universal final-week percentage. [^taper]
Confirm the route, feed stations, weather, travel, and start time. Pack the equipment and food you have already used in training.
Do not explain away unusual fatigue, pain, or illness as normal taper nerves. Tell your coach what changed so the race-day decision uses the information you have.

blocks.title: Race-week checklist
rows: Travel, start time, route and weather
Bike condition, familiar kit and food

items.title: Final Bike Check (Thursday or Friday)
items.content:
**Drivetrain:** Chain clean and lubed. Shifting smooth across all gears. No chain slip under power.

**Tires:** Tubeless sealant fresh. Tire pressure set for race conditions. Check for cuts, sidewall damage.

**Cockpit:** Computer charged and mounted. Bottles/cages secure. Bento box organized.

**Wheels:** Thru-axles tight. No spoke issues. Hubs spin smoothly.

**Don't:** Install new chain race week. Change tire pressure drastically. Add new untested equipment.

items.title: Race Day Bag (Pack Friday or Saturday)
items.content:
**Essentials:** Spare tube (even if tubeless), tire plugs, CO2 cartridges (2-3) or mini pump, multi-tool with chain breaker, quick link, tire levers.

**Nutrition:** Gels, bars, chews—whatever you practiced with. Bottle with sports drink pre-mixed. Extra water bottle.

**Other:** Sunscreen, chamois cream, arm warmers/vest, rain jacket (if forecast), extra base layer.

**Race essentials:** Bib number and pins, race chip, ID and emergency contact info.

blocks.content: Weather changes your gear strategy completely. A 55°F start with 15 mph wind feels very different from a 75°F calm morning—and your clothing choices should reflect that.
Scout the forecast Thursday morning. Lock in your plan by Friday. Do not second-guess Saturday morning—the stress of indecision costs more energy than being slightly overdressed.

sections.title: What Not to Do Race Week

blocks.content:
This is where most people sabotage themselves.

**Don't:** Get a massage Friday or Saturday. Try new equipment. Test your fitness. Experiment with nutrition (see [Chapter 5](#nutrition-fueling) for what works). Drink alcohol. Stay up late packing or stressing. Cut weight.

**Do:** Sleep 8-9 hours every night. Follow your taper plan exactly. Eat familiar foods. Finalize logistics early. Trust your training. Stay off social media if it makes you anxious. Review your race plan. Arrive at the start line fresh, fueled, and ready.

blocks.question: It's Thursday before your Saturday race. You feel sluggish and your legs feel heavy during an easy spin. What does this mean?

options.text: You've lost fitness during the taper — do a hard workout to test yourself
This is completely normal during taper week — trust the process and keep resting
You should increase carb intake dramatically to combat the fatigue

blocks.explanation: Taper-week sluggishness is universal. Your body is adapting to the reduced training load. Glycogen stores are filling up, muscle repair is happening. The heavy-leg feeling is not lost fitness—it's stored fitness waiting to be expressed. Athletes who panic and do a hard workout Thursday destroy their race. Trust the taper.

items.label: Gearing
items.detail: Use the gearing you need for the course in training before race week.

items.label: Braking and tyres
items.detail: Check condition, compatibility, and pressure using the tyre and wheel makers’ guidance.

items.label: Food and bottles
items.detail: Rehearse reaching, drinking, and carrying the food you will use.

items.label: Weather layers
items.detail: Plan what you carry on long descents and what you can remove safely.

sources.title: Bosquet et al. (2007) — Effects of tapering on performance

chapters.title: After the Finish
chapters.subtitle: Recovery, reflection, and building the next season

blocks.content: Recover before you schedule the next hard workout. The race duration, soreness, sleep, and any pain matter more than an arbitrary return date.
Write down what happened while you remember it. Separate the course conditions from your decisions: pacing, fueling, equipment, and positioning.
Choose one or two changes for the next training block. Keep the workouts and habits that worked, and give the next goal enough room on the calendar.

blocks.title: Debrief the race
rows: Where did effort stop matching the plan?
What did you consume and tolerate?
Which one or two changes matter?

tabs.label: Data Review
tabs.title: The Data Review
tabs.content:
Pull up your race file. Look at:

**Pacing:** Did you go out too hard? Did you fade in the second half? Did you finish strong?

**Power distribution:** What was your normalized power as % of {{FTP}}? Did it match your race plan?

**Heart rate:** Average HR as % of max? Did you redline early?

**Fueling execution:** Did you hit your target carb rate for the race duration? Any bonking or GI issues?

**Mechanicals:** Any flats, chain drops, failures? Could they have been prevented?

tabs.label: Honest Assessment
tabs.title: The Honest Assessment
tabs.content:
Ask yourself:

**What went well?** Pacing discipline? Fueling execution? Mental toughness? Equipment choices?

**What went poorly?** Blew up early? Under-fueled? Gave up mentally? Mechanical issues?

**What was in your control?** Training preparation, pacing decisions, fueling execution, equipment prep.

**What was outside your control?** Weather, course conditions, other riders' tactics.

Own what you could control. Learn from what went wrong. Don't make excuses for bad decisions.

tabs.label: Next Steps
tabs.title: Setting Your Next Goal
tabs.content:
**If you crushed it:** Move up a category. Target a harder race. Try longer distance.

**If you struggled:** Same category, better execution. More volume or consistency. Focus on the limiter.

**If you finished but didn't perform:** Analyze what went wrong. Adjust training approach.

One race is one data point. Don't overreact. But do learn.

blocks.content:
After you finish a race, there's often a void. You trained for months. It's over. Now what?

You need a new goal. Soon. Waiting too long leads to loss of motivation, inconsistent training, and fitness decay.

items.label: Pick a goal race
items.detail: Date, distance, location, difficulty level. Use the [Roadie Labs Race Database](/gravel-races/) to find your next target.

items.label: Define success
items.detail: Finish time, placement, or completion. Be realistic based on current fitness and what you learned from this race.

items.label: Work backward
items.detail: Race date minus 12 weeks = training start. Training start minus 4-8 weeks = off-season / recovery period.

items.label: Commit
items.detail: Register for the race. Tell people. Make it real. The goal isn't just aspirational—it's a commitment.

items.label: Before the group split
items.detail: Were you positioned safely, and did you recognise the course change?

items.label: During the climb
items.detail: Did the effort match your plan or the wheel in front?

items.label: After the descent
items.detail: Did your line and braking leave you in control?

items.label: For the next block
items.detail: Choose the training or skill that addresses the recorded problem.

glossary.FTP: Functional Threshold Power — the max watts you can sustain for ~1 hour
glossary.CTL: Chronic Training Load — your fitness trend over 42 days
glossary.ATL: Acute Training Load — your fatigue trend over 7 days
glossary.TSB: Training Stress Balance — CTL minus ATL. Positive = fresh, negative = fatigued
glossary.TSS: Training Stress Score — how hard a single workout was relative to your FTP
glossary.IF: Intensity Factor — ratio of workout power to FTP
glossary.NP: Normalized Power — weighted average power accounting for variability
glossary.RPE: Rate of Perceived Exertion — subjective effort on a 1-10 scale
glossary.Z2: Zone 2 — easy aerobic pace, 55-75% of FTP. The foundation of endurance
glossary.VO2max: Maximum oxygen uptake — your aerobic ceiling, trainable by ~15%
glossary.PMC: Performance Management Chart — plots CTL, ATL, and TSB over time
glossary.DOMS: Delayed Onset Muscle Soreness — peaks 24-72 hours after hard efforts
glossary.W/kg: Watts per kilogram — power-to-weight ratio, the key metric for climbing
glossary.DNF: Did Not Finish — dropping out of a race
glossary.bonk: Hitting the wall — when glycogen stores deplete and performance collapses
